job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Aaron Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at seven, walk twenty minutes to Harcourt and Dean, a small accountancy practice with six staff in Wexton. I do bookkeeping, bank reconciliations and VAT returns for local shops and tradesmen, and I'm studying for my professional exams in the evenings. I did an accounting degree and passed, without any internships, and I rent a flat with my cousin Dev. On Thursdays I play five-a-side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I figured. Most of the hype I've seen has been people selling something. At work I'd say nothing, we'd carry on with the books like always. With friends I'd shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm glad. I've got a job I understand at Harcourt and Dean, a small accountancy practice with six staff, and I've started my professional exams. I like things that stay put long enough for me to get good at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing bookkeeping and VAT returns for local shops and tradesmen, and sit my first two exam papers this year. I'd pay 200 a month toward my student loan and put 100 aside. I'd keep living in the flat I share with my cousin Dev, and go to the five-a-side on Thursdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy. I'd feel pretty normal, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the butcher closing. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What worries me a little, even here, is that our clients are small shops and a lot of them are folding anyway. A butcher we do the books for closed last month. That's a more real worry than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would taking on the payroll side involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I lost clients, the firm would have less work for a junior. I'd ask my boss Gerald whether I could take on the payroll side. A small practice can only keep someone who finds something useful to do.

say: I'd say it's about what I **figured**, since most hype I've seen is people selling something.
At work I'd say **nothing** and carry on with the books.
think: I'm **glad**, because I understand my job and like things staying put while I get good.
The real worry is **small clients** closing, like the butcher last month.
do: Sit my first **two exam papers** this year.
Pay **200 a month** on the loan and put 100 aside.
Ask boss Gerald about taking on the **payroll** side.
feel: I'd feel **easy** and normal, which is how I like it.
S0.quote: A small practice can only keep someone who finds something useful to do.
fieldNote: Aaron's calm is tied to **familiarity**; he likes a job that stays put while he builds skill.
His real pressure is **local business** closures, which would cut work for a junior at a six-person practice.

steps.text: Sit two professional exam papers this year
Pay 200 a month toward the student loan
Ask Gerald to let me take on payroll

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's wait and see how much of it is real, and we shouldn't rush into anything. At work I'd say our clients still want a person to explain their tax. Online I'd stay out of it, since people fight there for sport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I think the simple stuff I do is exactly what gets automated: data entry, reconciling bank statements, sorting receipts. I don't use any AI tools, and I'm not keen to. But Gerald might decide he needs fewer juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the work the old way as long as I'm allowed, and push on with my exams, because a chartered qualification is worth something no matter how the tools go. If Gerald tells me to use the tools, I'd learn them slowly with the senior, Moira. I'd also stop buying lunch out and save about 250 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I don't love being told to change how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gerald if he told you to start using the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, Istvan, is an electrician, and he thinks anything on a screen is a bit of a con. But he'd say get your qualification and stay useful. That's about my own view too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your clients would still pay for a person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I can't see is whether clients will pay for a person once software gives them a quote in a minute. Some will, I think, the older ones. But my generation of clients might not.

say: I'd say clients still want a **person** to explain their tax.
I'd say let's **wait and see** how much of it is real.
think: The simple work I do, like reconciling statements and sorting receipts, is what gets **automated**.
Gerald might decide he needs **fewer** juniors.
do: Keep going with **exams**, because a chartered qualification holds value whatever the tools do.
Learn the tools **slowly** with Moira if Gerald asks.
Save about **250 a month** and stop buying lunch.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy**, since I don't love being told to change how I work.
S1.quote: A chartered qualification is worth something no matter how the tools go.
fieldNote: Aaron resists tools but protects himself with a **qualification**, which fits his careful nature.
His open question is whether young clients will **pay** for a person once quotes arrive in a minute.

steps.text: Keep working through the chartered exam papers
Learn the firm's software slowly with Moira
Save 250 a month by skipping lunches out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and somebody has to slow it down. At work I'd ask Gerald straight out whether the firm has a plan. With friends I'd say honestly that I don't know what to do, and I don't think anyone does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the job I'm training for may not be there by the time I've qualified. The exams take three more years. If AGI arrives by 2028, I'd be halfway through a qualification for work that a machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending hard, move to a cheaper room, and push my savings from 100 to 350 a month. I'd stop the exams at the next fee, 900, until I knew more. I'd ask my dad whether his electrician firm needs a bookkeeper or an apprentice, since the hands-on side gets three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty bad. I like a plan, and this takes the plan away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum, Judit, when you told her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum, Judit, that I've got a degree that might be worth less than we thought, and she'd cry a bit and then say we'll manage. We always did. She could lend me a few hundred, and she'd cook for me on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to stop the exams halfway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part that gets me is how little control there is. I can't out-work a machine, and I'm not good at guessing what comes next. So I'd lean on the people I know and keep my costs low.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and somebody has to slow it down.
I'd ask Gerald straight out whether the firm has a **plan**.
think: The job I'm training for may not exist by the time I've **qualified**.
I can't **out-work** a machine, and I'm not good at guessing what comes next.
do: Cut spending and **move** to a cheaper room, saving 350 a month.
Pause the **exams** at the next 900 fee until I know more.
Ask my dad whether his electrician firm needs a **bookkeeper or apprentice**.
feel: I'd feel **bad**, because I like a plan and this takes the plan away.
S2.quote: I can't out-work a machine, and I'm not good at guessing what comes next.
fieldNote: Aaron expects his **career path** to collapse before the exams finish, and he says he cannot out-work a machine.
He turns to **family** and the trades, which hold out three more years.

steps.text: Pause the exams at the next 900 fee
Save 350 a month in a cheaper room
Ask dad about bookkeeping or apprentice work at his electrician firm
Lean on mum Judit for Sunday meals and a loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, but it's long enough to make a decent plan. At work I'd ask Gerald to talk it through with us. I'd keep my opinions off the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be nervous but I think I could still land somewhere. I might not be an accountant at the end, but I'd be something. My worry is that I'm slow to learn new things, and I'd know it by year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the exams in the first three years, then look for work that sits next to accounts but needs a person, like advising small business owners face to face. I'd save 250 a month and keep my costs low. Starting in year two I'd learn the firm's software properly, with Moira's help, as a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, about as manageable as a mountain looks from the bottom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your cousin Dev suggest, and what do you make of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, my cousin, thinks I should become a financial adviser. I think there's something in it. People trust a face, and I don't know yet whether they'd trust a younger man with no track record. That's the open question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the risk in finishing the exams?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If five years turns into three, I'd have wasted the exam fees. That's a risk I'd take, because the qualification still opens doors. A piece of paper isn't nothing.

say: I'd say five years isn't long, but long enough to make a **decent plan**.
I'd ask Gerald to talk it through with the **team**.
think: I'm **nervous**, but I think I could still land somewhere, even if not as an accountant.
I'm slow to learn new things, and I'd **know** it by year two.
do: Finish the **exams** in three years, then move into face-to-face small business advice.
Save **250 a month** and keep costs low.
Learn the firm's **software** properly with Moira's help from year two.
feel: It's **manageable**, about as manageable as a mountain looks from the bottom.
S3.quote: People trust a face, and I don't know yet whether they'd trust a younger man with no track record.
fieldNote: Aaron plans a **bridge** from accounting to advising, built on people trusting a face.
He knows his own **slowness** with new tools and tries to start early because of it.

steps.text: Finish the chartered exams within three years
Learn the firm's software with Moira from year two
Move toward advising small business owners face to face
Save 250 a month and keep costs low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot of things can change in it, including this. At work I'd keep doing my job. With friends I'd say don't panic, just don't do nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. I'd be 32, probably qualified and maybe with my own small client list. Ten years is enough to find a corner that machines don't want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work through the exams, build my client base in the firm, and keep saving 200 a month toward a deposit on a flat. I'd learn the tools only once they're proven in my line of work, and not before. I'd stay in touch with Dev and Moira, so I'd hear early if the firm changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I know I'm the kind who waits, and with ten years that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the kind who waits. When does waiting stop being a good idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get complacent, and I know it. If I hear from the senior staff that the work is shrinking, I'd jump on it faster. I'd set myself a check every January to ask what's changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you trust to tell you what's real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would help is clear news from my own profession, such as the chartered body saying what's real and what isn't. I don't trust the headlines. I trust the exam board to tell me where the work is going.

say: I'd say ten years is long and a lot can change, **including this**.
I'd tell friends **don't panic**, but don't do nothing.
think: I'd be **fine**: 32, probably qualified, maybe with my own small client list.
Ten years is enough to find a **corner** machines don't want.
do: Work through the **exams** and build my client base in the firm.
Save **200 a month** toward a flat deposit.
Learn the tools once they're **proven** in my line of work.
feel: I'd feel **mostly calm**, since waiting works when there's time.
S4.quote: I don't trust the headlines. I trust the exam board to tell me where the work is going.
fieldNote: Aaron's **waiting** style suits the long horizon, and he sets a January check to guard against complacency.
He trusts his **professional body** more than headlines to say where the work is going.

steps.text: Pass the chartered exams and build a client list
Save 200 a month toward a flat deposit
Check each January what has changed in the firm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, by a mile. I'd be halfway through exams for a job that might be gone, and I'm not quick at picking up new things. What would help is clear word from my professional body, some money for retraining, and my firm being honest about what it plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that I'm not against any of this, I just like to understand something before I use it. Some of us need more time, and that shouldn't count against us.

headlineQuote: Some of us need more time, and that shouldn't count against us.
portrait: Aaron is an accounting graduate, four months into a bookkeeping job at a six-person practice, **renting** with his cousin.
He is a centrist and a resistant adopter who uses no AI tools and likes the familiar.
His mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** as warning time shrinks, and he leans on exams, family and the trades.
He is slow to change, so longer warning matters a great deal to him.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most: he'd be halfway through exams for work that might be gone.
whatWouldHelp: Clear word from his **professional body**, retraining money, and an honest plan from his firm.
